passages.title: Loss and the return to Bethlehem
passages.summary: In the days of the judges a famine strikes Bethlehem. Elimelech takes his wife Naomi and two sons to Moab. He dies, and the sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. After about ten years both sons die. Naomi hears there is food in Judah and starts home. She tells her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. Orpah leaves, but Ruth promises to share Naomi’s people, God, and grave. They reach Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest.
passages.uncertainty: The points show Bethlehem and the region of Moab. The Moab point marks a region, not a town.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Ruth's loyalty and faith during loss. What does Ruth promise in verses 16–17, and what does it cost her?

contextNote.title: A changed name expresses an argument about loss
contextNote.text: Naomi returns to a town that still knows her name (verse 19). She asks to be called Mara, and the verse ties that name to bitterness. She blames the Almighty directly in verses 20–21. She left full, she says, and the LORD brought her back empty. Ruth stands beside her as she says “empty.” The book lets the complaint stand without any rebuke. Verse 22 then quietly adds two things: Ruth and the harvest.

passages.title: Ruth gleans in Boaz’s field
passages.summary: Ruth asks Naomi to let her gather leftover grain behind the harvesters. She happens to come to the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech. Boaz asks who she is, and the foreman reports her request and steady work. Boaz tells her to stay in his field and drink from his water. He has heard what she did for Naomi. He shares his meal and tells his men to leave extra stalks for her. Ruth carries home a large measure of barley. Naomi blesses Boaz and says he is a close relative.
passages.uncertainty: The points show Bethlehem and the region of Moab. The Moab point marks a region, not a town.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies kindness and trust. Consider how practical help changes the conditions another person faces. What does Boaz add in verses 15–16 beyond what Ruth asked?

contextNote.title: A harvest rule becomes a means of survival
contextNote.text: The law left the edges of a field for the poor and the foreigner. Leviticus 19:9–10 and Deuteronomy 24:19 state the rule. Ruth is both, and in verse 7 she still asks permission. Verses 9 and 22 show why: a woman alone in a field risked harm. Boaz first gives what the law requires and then more. He orders his men to pull stalks out for her (verse 16). In verse 20 Naomi’s speech changes, and she blesses the LORD’s kindness.

passages.title: The request at the threshing floor
passages.summary: Naomi wants a secure home for Ruth. She sends her to the threshing floor where Boaz winnows barley at night. Ruth washes, dresses, and waits until he has eaten and lies down. She uncovers his feet and lies there. At midnight he wakes and asks who she is. She asks him to spread his garment over her as a near kinsman. Boaz blesses her and promises to act, but a nearer kinsman has first right. He sends her home before dawn with six measures of barley.
passages.uncertainty: The points show Bethlehem and the region of Moab. The Moab point marks a region, not a town.

lds.text: The older Church manual reads Ruth's action as a request for marriage. How do Ruth’s words in verse 9 differ from Naomi’s plan in verse 4?

contextNote.title: Ruth gives the plan her own words
contextNote.text: Naomi’s plan ends with Boaz telling Ruth what to do (verse 4). In verse 9 Ruth tells Boaz what to do. She asks for his covering and gives the reason: he is a near kinsman. That ties her marriage to his family duty toward Naomi’s house. In 2:12 Boaz prayed that the LORD would shelter her. Now she asks him to be that shelter. Boaz calls her request a kindness and names her a worthy woman (verses 10–11).

passages.title: The gate agreement and Obed’s birth
passages.summary: Boaz sits at the town gate and stops the nearer kinsman. He gathers ten elders as witnesses. He says Naomi is selling Elimelech’s field, and the man agrees to buy it. Boaz adds that the buyer must marry Ruth and raise an heir for the dead. The man withdraws and hands over his sandal to confirm it. Boaz declares that he has bought the land and taken Ruth as his wife. Ruth bears Obed, and the women tell Naomi her life is restored. Obed becomes the grandfather of David.
passages.uncertainty: The points show Bethlehem and the region of Moab. The Moab point marks a region, not a town.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares Boaz’s care with Jesus Christ’s power to redeem, or save. How does Boaz help Ruth and Naomi?

contextNote.title: Care requires a public commitment
contextNote.text: The gate is the town’s court, and ten elders make the act public. The nearer kinsman accepts the field (verse 4) and refuses Ruth (verse 6). A son by Ruth would carry Mahlon’s name and inherit the land. Boaz accepts that cost in verses 9–10 before witnesses. The man who guarded his own estate is never named in the book. A cuneiform tablet shows how another people recorded a field sale. The women tell Naomi that Ruth is better than seven sons (verse 15).

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

regions.name: Tribes of Israel · approximate
regions.summary: Israel’s tribes held hill country on both sides of the Jordan. No king ruled them all before Saul.
regions.detail: Joshua divides the land by tribe. In Judges each tribe faces its own enemies, and Saul first draws them together.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Judges 1 lists towns the tribes did not take. Some scholars doubt the twelve-tribe picture.

regions.name: Moab · approximate
regions.summary: Moab was a kingdom on the high land east of the Dead Sea. Dibon was its capital.
regions.detail: Eglon of Moab rules Israel for eighteen years until Ehud kills him (Judges 3). Ruth comes from Moab.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Numbers 21:26 says Moab once lost land north of the Arnon.

chapterMaps.narrative: In the days of the judges a famine strikes Bethlehem. Elimelech takes his wife Naomi and two sons to Moab. He dies, and the sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. After about ten years both sons die. Naomi hears there is food in Judah and starts home. She tells her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. Orpah leaves, but Ruth promises to share Naomi’s people, God, and grave. They reach Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest.

chapterMaps.narrative: Ruth asks Naomi to let her gather leftover grain behind the harvesters. She happens to come to the field of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech. Boaz asks who she is, and the foreman reports her request and steady work. Boaz tells her to stay in his field and drink from his water. He has heard what she did for Naomi. He shares his meal and tells his men to leave extra stalks for her. Ruth carries home a large measure of barley. Naomi blesses Boaz and says he is a close relative.

chapterMaps.narrative: Naomi wants a secure home for Ruth. She sends her to the threshing floor where Boaz winnows barley at night. Ruth washes, dresses, and waits until he has eaten and lies down. She uncovers his feet and lies there. At midnight he wakes and asks who she is. She asks him to spread his garment over her as a near kinsman. Boaz blesses her and promises to act, but a nearer kinsman has first right. He sends her home before dawn with six measures of barley.

chapterMaps.narrative: Boaz sits at the town gate and stops the nearer kinsman. He gathers ten elders as witnesses. He says Naomi is selling Elimelech’s field, and the man agrees to buy it. Boaz adds that the buyer must marry Ruth and raise an heir for the dead. The man withdraws and hands over his sandal to confirm it. Boaz declares that he has bought the land and taken Ruth as his wife. Ruth bears Obed, and the women tell Naomi her life is restored. Obed becomes the grandfather of David.

textRoutes.title: Loss and the return to Bethlehem
textRoutes.summary: In the days of the judges a famine strikes Bethlehem. Elimelech takes his wife Naomi and two sons to Moab. He dies, and the sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. After about ten years both sons die. Naomi hears there is food in Judah and starts home. She tells her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. Orpah leaves, but Ruth promises to share Naomi’s people, God, and grave. They reach Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest.
textRoutes.detail: Naomi returns to a town that still knows her name (verse 19). She asks to be called Mara, and the verse ties that name to bitterness. She blames the Almighty directly in verses 20–21. She left full, she says, and the LORD brought her back empty. Ruth stands beside her as she says “empty.” The book lets the complaint stand without any rebuke. Verse 22 then quietly adds two things: Ruth and the harvest.
